Let \(q=3^r\). Since \(L\cap F=0\), write \(L=\{x+Sx:x\in E\}\). The Lagrangian condition gives \(S=S^T\), and \(\iota(L)=L\) gives \(S\) commuting with the reversal matrix. Hence
\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&c&d\\
b&e&h&c\\
c&h&e&b\\
d&c&b&a
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The three stated linear conditions imply
\[
a=1,\qquad e+2c=0,\qquad d+h=b.
\]
Since the field has characteristic \(3\), \(e=c\), so
\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}
1&b&c&d\\
b&c&b-d&c\\
c&b-d&c&b\\
d&c&b&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
with \(b,c,d\in\mathbb F_q\). Thus only the condition involving \(\rho_t\) remains.

Put
\[
u_t=(1,t,t^2,t^3)^T.
\]
For \(x+Sx\in L\), its image under \(\rho_t\) has zero \(E\)-component exactly when \(x\) is a scalar multiple of \(u_t\) and
\[
u_t^T S u_t=0.
\]
Therefore \(\rho_t(L)\cap F=0\) for every \(t\in\mathbb F_q\) iff
\[
u_t^T S u_t\neq 0
\]
for every \(t\in\mathbb F_q\). A direct computation gives
\[
u_t^T S u_t=t^6-b(t^5+t^3+t)+1.
\]
The variables \(c,d\) do not appear, so they contribute a factor \(q^2\).

For \(t=0,\pm1\), the above polynomial is never zero. For \(t\neq0,\pm1\), the bad values of \(b\) are
\[
b=\frac{t^6+1}{t^5+t^3+t}.
\]
Using \(y=t+t^{-1}\), this becomes
\[
b=\frac{y^3}{y^2-1}.
\]
Here \(y\) ranges over those elements with \(y^2-1\) a nonzero square.

The map
\[
g(y)=\frac{y^3}{y^2-1}
\]
has fibers given by the order-\(3\) transformation
\[
T(y)=\frac{y}{y+1},
\]
because
\[
g(y)=g(z)
\]
implies \(z=y\), \(z=T(y)\), or \(z=T^2(y)\).

Let \(\chi\) be the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_q\). The domain is
\[
Y=\{y:\chi(y^2-1)=1\}.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_q}\chi(y^2-1)=-1,
\]
we have
\[
|Y|=\frac{q-3}{2}.
\]

If \(r\) is odd, then \(-1\) is nonsquare. Each relevant \(T\)-orbit meeting \(Y\) contains exactly two points of \(Y\), so the number of bad \(b\)'s is
\[
\frac{|Y|}{2}=\frac{q-3}{4}.
\]
Thus the number of good \(b\)'s is
\[
q-\frac{q-3}{4}=\frac{3(q+1)}4.
\]

If \(r\) is even, then \(-1\) is square. The fixed point \(y=0\) contributes one bad value, and every other relevant \(T\)-orbit contributes one bad value. Hence the number of bad \(b\)'s is
\[
1+\frac{q-3}{3}=\frac q3.
\]
Thus the number of good \(b\)'s is
\[
q-\frac q3=\frac{2q}{3}.
\]

Multiplying by the free choices of \(c,d\), we get
\[
\boxed{
M_r=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{3q^2(q+1)}4,& r\ \text{odd},\\[6pt]
\dfrac{2q^3}{3},& r\ \text{even},
\end{cases}
\qquad q=3^r.
}
\]
